bookSections.title: Identify, Describe, Classify and Sketch Quadrilaterals
Classify, Estimate, Measure and Draw Angles

preamble.whatYouWillLearn: You will describe and sort quadrilaterals by their sides, angles, parallel sides, diagonals and symmetry. You will learn the parts of a circle and how to draw one with compasses. You will work out the area of triangles, classify and measure angles, and use the facts that angles add up to 180° on a straight line, 360° around a point and 180° in a triangle.
preamble.whyItMatters: Shapes and angles are the language of building, design and maps. Knowing the angle facts lets you work out angles you cannot measure. Finding the area of triangles helps with floors, gardens and any shape made of straight edges.
realWorld: Cutting a round kuih or a pizza into equal slices from the centre
Checking that a door frame or photo frame is a true rectangle by measuring its two diagonals
Working out how many tiles cover a triangular corner of a room
Marking out a round flower bed with a peg and a piece of string, like giant compasses
Setting a ramp or a ladder at a safe angle

subtopics.title: Quadrilaterals and their properties
subtopics.summary: Square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, trapezium and kite: their sides, angles, parallel sides, diagonals and lines of symmetry.

subtopics.title: Circles
subtopics.summary: The centre, radius, diameter and circumference of a circle, and drawing a circle of a given radius or diameter with compasses.

subtopics.title: Area of right-angled triangles
subtopics.summary: A right-angled triangle is half of a rectangle, so its area is half of length x width. Use this to find areas of shapes made of rectangles and triangles.

subtopics.title: Angles
subtopics.summary: Acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex angles; estimating and measuring with a protractor; angles on a straight line (180°) and around a point (360°).

subtopics.title: Angles in a triangle
subtopics.summary: The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°. Use this, and the facts about isosceles and equilateral triangles, to find missing angles.

questions.prompt: Which quadrilateral ALWAYS has four equal sides and four right angles?
questions.solution: Check both clues. Four equal sides: a square or a rhombus. Four right angles: a square or a rectangle. Only the square always has both.

misconceptions.0: A rhombus always has four equal sides, but its angles do not have to be right angles. It can look like a square that has been pushed over.
misconceptions.2: A rectangle always has four right angles, but its sides do not all have to be equal. Usually two sides are long and two are short.
misconceptions.3: A kite has two pairs of equal sides that are next to each other, not four equal sides, and it does not have to have any right angles.

questions.prompt: True or false: Every square is also a rectangle.
questions.solution: A rectangle is a quadrilateral with four right angles and opposite sides equal. A square has four right angles, and its opposite sides are equal (in fact all four sides are equal). So a square is a special kind of rectangle. The statement is true.

misconceptions.common: Thinking a rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides. That is the picture we usually draw, but it is not part of the definition.

questions.prompt: A quadrilateral has exactly one pair of parallel sides. What is it called?
questions.solution: Count the pairs of parallel sides. Parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle and square have 2 pairs. A kite has none. A trapezium has exactly 1 pair.

misconceptions.0: A parallelogram has TWO pairs of parallel sides: each side is parallel to the side opposite it.
misconceptions.1: A kite (that is not a rhombus) has no parallel sides at all. Its equal sides are next to each other.
misconceptions.2: A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides, so it has two pairs of parallel sides, not one.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the quadrilaterals whose two diagonals ALWAYS cross at right angles.
questions.solution: Square: yes, its diagonals are equal and cross at right angles. Rhombus: yes, its diagonals cross at right angles. Kite: yes, one diagonal crosses the other at a right angle. Rectangle and parallelogram: not always. So the answers are square, rhombus and kite.

misconceptions.1: A rectangle's diagonals are equal and cut each other in half, but they only cross at right angles when the rectangle is a square.
misconceptions.4: A parallelogram's diagonals cut each other in half, but in an ordinary parallelogram they do not cross at right angles.

questions.prompt: Shapes A, B, C and D are drawn on the squared grid. Match each shape to its number of lines of symmetry.
questions.solution: First name each shape by counting squares. A is a parallelogram (opposite sides parallel, no right angles, a long pair and a short pair of sides). B is a square. C is a kite (two long sides meet at the bottom and two short sides meet at the top). D is a rhombus (every side goes 3 across and 2 up or down, so all four sides are equal, but it has no right angles). Now count the lines of symmetry. A, parallelogram: 0 lines, because no fold makes the two halves sit exactly on top of each other. B, square: 4 lines (two through opposite corners, two through the middles of opposite sides). C, kite: 1 line, the upright line through its top and bottom corners. D, rhombus: 2 lines, along both diagonals.

misconceptions.common: Thinking a diagonal of the parallelogram (shape A) is a line of symmetry. If you fold a paper parallelogram along a diagonal, the two halves do not match. Also check the kite (shape C): only the line through the corners where the equal sides meet works.

questions.prompt: A quadrilateral has two pairs of equal sides. The equal sides are next to each other (not opposite each other), and the shape has no parallel sides. What is this quadrilateral called?
questions.solution: Two pairs of equal sides that are next to each other, with no parallel sides, is a kite. (A dented, arrow-shaped kite is called an arrowhead; it is a special kind of kite.)

misconceptions.common: Calling it a parallelogram. In a parallelogram the equal sides are opposite each other and parallel; in a kite the equal sides are next to each other.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a parallelogram with one angle of 70°. In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal, and the four angles of any quadrilateral add up to 360°. What is the size of the angle marked ? (the angle next to the 70° angle)? Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: The angle opposite the 70° angle is also 70°. 70 + 70 = 140. The other two angles share 360 - 140 = 220°, and they are equal, so each is 220 ÷ 2 = 110°. The angle marked ? is one of them: 110°. Check: 70 + 110 = 180. Angles next to each other in a parallelogram always add up to 180°.

misconceptions.common: Answering 70° by thinking all the angles of a parallelogram are equal. Only OPPOSITE angles are equal; look at the drawing: the angle marked ? is wider than the 70° angle. Angles next to each other add up to 180°.

questions.prompt: Mei Lin describes a quadrilateral: 'Its two diagonals are the same length and cut each other exactly in half, but they do NOT cross at right angles.' Which shape is she describing?
questions.solution: Equal diagonals that cut each other in half: rectangle or square. Not at right angles rules out the square. So it is a rectangle (one that is not a square).

misconceptions.1: A square's diagonals are equal and cut each other in half, but they DO cross at right angles, so it does not fit the last clue.
misconceptions.2: A rhombus's diagonals cross at right angles, and they are usually different lengths.
misconceptions.3: An isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals, but they do not cut each other in half: they cross nearer to the shorter parallel side.

questions.prompt: Look at the circle. What is the name of the straight line marked ?, which goes from the centre of the circle to its edge?

diagram.alt: A circle with its centre marked. A straight line marked ? goes from the centre to the edge of the circle.

questions.solution: The line marked ? starts at the centre and ends on the edge, so it is a radius. Two radii in a straight line make a diameter.

misconceptions.0: A diameter goes from edge to edge THROUGH the centre, so it is twice as long as a radius.
misconceptions.1: The circumference is the distance all the way round the circle, not a line from the centre.
misconceptions.3: The centre is the middle point of the circle, not a line.

questions.prompt: Look at the circle. Its radius is 7 cm, as marked. How long is the diameter marked ? on the drawing?
questions.solution: The diameter goes right across the circle through the centre, so it is two radii long. Diameter = 2 x radius = 2 x 7 = 14 cm.

misconceptions.0: You halved the radius. The diameter is twice the radius, so double it: 7 x 2 = 14 cm.
misconceptions.1: You thought the radius and diameter are the same. The diameter goes right across the circle through the centre, so it is two radii long.
misconceptions.3: You multiplied by 3, perhaps remembering 'about 3 times' from the circumference. The diameter is simply 2 radii: 7 + 7 = 14 cm.

questions.prompt: You want to draw a circle with a diameter of 9 cm using a pair of compasses. How far apart should you open the compasses, from the point to the pencil tip?
questions.solution: The compasses' point sits on the centre and the pencil draws the edge, so the gap is the radius. Radius = diameter ÷ 2 = 9 ÷ 2 = 4.5 cm.

misconceptions.1: You opened the compasses to the diameter. The gap between the point (the centre) and the pencil (the edge) is the radius, which is half the diameter.
misconceptions.2: You doubled instead of halving. The radius is half of the diameter: 9 ÷ 2 = 4.5 cm.
misconceptions.3: You divided by 3. The radius is half the diameter, so divide by 2: 9 ÷ 2 = 4.5 cm.

questions.prompt: Look at the circle. O is its centre, and A, B and C are points on its edge. Match each part of the drawing to its name.

diagram.alt: A circle with centre O. Points A, B and C are on the circle. A straight line joins A to B and passes through O. Another straight line joins O to C.

left: the curved line all the way round

questions.solution: O is the point in the middle, the same distance from every point on the edge: the centre. OC goes from the centre to the edge: a radius. AB goes from edge to edge THROUGH the centre O: a diameter (two radii, OA and OB, in a straight line). The curved line all the way round is the circumference. (A chord is a line joining two points on the edge that does NOT pass through the centre; there is none here.)

misconceptions.common: Mixing up radius and diameter. The diameter (AB) goes all the way across through the centre; the radius (OC) goes only halfway, from the centre to the edge. Calling AB a chord: a line from edge to edge that passes through the centre is called a diameter.

questions.prompt: True or false: Any straight line that joins two points on the edge of a circle is a diameter.
questions.solution: A diameter must pass through the centre. A line from edge to edge that misses the centre is shorter than the diameter (it is called a chord). So the statement is false.

misconceptions.common: Forgetting that a diameter must go through the centre of the circle.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the tool you use to draw a circle with an exact radius?
questions.solution: A pair of compasses has a sharp point that stays on the centre and a pencil that draws the edge. You open it to the radius you want.

misconceptions.common: Saying a protractor. A protractor measures angles; compasses draw circles.

questions.prompt: Four identical circles are drawn in a row inside a rectangle. Each circle touches the circles next to it. Every circle touches both long sides of the rectangle, and the two end circles also touch the short sides. Each circle has a radius of 3 cm. How long is the rectangle?
questions.solution: Diameter = 2 x 3 = 6 cm. The four circles sit side by side, so the length is 4 diameters: 4 x 6 = 24 cm.

misconceptions.0: You used the radius instead of the diameter: 4 x 3 = 12 cm. Each circle takes up a full diameter (6 cm) of the length.
misconceptions.1: You measured from the centre of the first circle to the centre of the last one (3 diameters). You also need a radius at each end: 18 + 3 + 3 = 24 cm.
misconceptions.2: 6 cm is one diameter, which is the WIDTH of the rectangle, not its length.

questions.prompt: A circle is drawn inside a square so that it just touches all four sides of the square. The perimeter of the square is 36 cm. What is the radius of the circle? Give your answer in cm.
questions.solution: Side of the square = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm. The circle touches two opposite sides, so its diameter is the same as the side: 9 cm. Radius = 9 ÷ 2 = 4.5 cm.

misconceptions.common: Answering 9 cm. That is the diameter (the same as the side of the square); the radius is half of it.

questions.prompt: Look at the angle drawn below. It measures 135°. What type of angle is it?
questions.solution: 135° is more than 90° (a right angle) but less than 180° (a straight line), so it is an obtuse angle. In the drawing the arms open wider than a square corner but not into a straight line.

misconceptions.0: Acute angles are less than 90°. 135° is bigger than a right angle.
misconceptions.2: Reflex angles are more than 180°. 135° is less than a straight line.
misconceptions.3: A straight angle is exactly 180°.

questions.prompt: Put these types of angle in order of size, from smallest to largest.
questions.solution: Acute: less than 90°. Right: exactly 90°. Obtuse: between 90° and 180°. Straight: exactly 180°. Reflex: between 180° and 360°.

misconceptions.common: Putting reflex before straight. A reflex angle is MORE than 180°, so it is bigger than a straight angle.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows two angles next to each other on a straight line. What is the size of the angle marked ? on the drawing? Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. 180 - 48 = 132°.

misconceptions.common: Using 90° or 360° instead of 180°. A straight line is a half turn, so the angles on it add up to 180°.

questions.prompt: A protractor is placed on the angle as shown, with its centre on the corner of the angle and one arm along the zero line. What is the size of the angle?
questions.solution: Find the arm that lies along the zero line: it points to the RIGHT. Use the scale that starts at 0 on the right (the inner scale). Follow it round to the other arm: it reads 40. (The outer scale reads 140 there, but that scale starts at 0 on the left.) Check: the angle is smaller than a right angle, so it is acute and 40° fits. The angle is 40°.

misconceptions.1: You read the wrong scale. The arm on the zero line points to the right, so use the scale that starts at 0 on the right. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so it must be less than 90°.
misconceptions.2: You took 40 from 360. That gives the reflex angle on the outside of the arms, not the angle between them.
misconceptions.3: You worked out how far the arm is from a right angle (90 - 40). The protractor reading already gives the angle.

questions.prompt: Three angles meet at a point, as shown in the diagram. What is the size of the angle marked ? on the drawing?
questions.solution: Angles around a point add up to 360°. 110 + 95 = 205. 360 - 205 = 155°.

misconceptions.0: You added the two angles but did not take the total away from 360°.
misconceptions.1: Slip in 360 - 205. In the ones column, 0 - 5 needs an exchange: 360 - 205 = 155, not 165.
misconceptions.3: You used 180° (a straight line) instead of 360°. Angles around a point make a full turn of 360°.

questions.prompt: True or false: An angle of 190° is a reflex angle.
questions.solution: A reflex angle is bigger than 180° and smaller than 360°. 190° is in that range, so it is reflex. The statement is true.

misconceptions.common: Thinking only angles close to 360° are reflex. Any angle between 180° and 360° is reflex.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the angles that are acute.
questions.solution: Acute angles are less than 90°. 89°, 12° and 45° are acute. 90° is a right angle; 91° and 179° are obtuse.

misconceptions.1: 90° is exactly a right angle. Acute means LESS than 90°.
misconceptions.3: 91° is just over a right angle, so it is obtuse.
misconceptions.5: 179° is between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse (nearly a straight line).

questions.prompt: Arjun measured the angle shown with his protractor and wrote down 65°. He had read the wrong scale. What is the real size of the angle?
questions.solution: The arm on the zero line points to the right, so the correct scale is the one that starts at 0 on the right (the inner scale). On that scale the other arm passes 115. Arjun read 65 from the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The angle is clearly obtuse (wider than a right angle), so 65° cannot be right. Check: the two scales add up to 180° at every mark: 180 - 65 = 115°.

misconceptions.0: You took 65 from 90. The two scales on a protractor always add up to 180°, so the other reading is 180 - 65.
misconceptions.2: You took 65 from 360, which gives a reflex angle. The angle is obtuse, so it is between 90° and 180°.
misconceptions.3: That is Arjun's wrong reading. An obtuse angle must be bigger than 90°.

questions.prompt: Four angles meet at a point, as shown. The three angles marked x are equal. What is the size of each angle x?
questions.solution: Angles around a point add up to 360°. 360 - 120 = 240. The three equal angles x share 240°: 240 ÷ 3 = 80°. Check: 120 + 80 + 80 + 80 = 360.

misconceptions.0: You found 360 - 120 = 240 but forgot to share it equally among the three angles.
misconceptions.1: You used 180° instead of 360°: (180 - 120) ÷ 3 = 20. Angles around a point add up to 360°.
misconceptions.2: You assumed all four angles are the same size. Check: 4 x 120 = 480, which is more than 360°.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows three angles, a, b and c, on a straight line. Angle a is 35°. Angle b is twice the size of angle a. What is the size of angle c? Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: b = 2 x 35 = 70°. a + b = 35 + 70 = 105°. Angles on a straight line add up to 180°, so c = 180 - 105 = 75°.

misconceptions.common: Forgetting to double: 180 - 35 - 35 = 110°. Angle b is twice angle a, so b = 70°.

questions.prompt: Look at the angle drawn below. Which is the best estimate of its size?

diagram.alt: Two arms meet at a point. The angle between them is marked, and it is a little narrower than a square corner.

questions.solution: Compare the angle with a right angle (90°), the corner of a square. The arms are not quite as wide apart as a square corner, so the angle is a little smaller than 90°. About 80° is the best estimate.

misconceptions.0: 100° is a little BIGGER than a right angle (it is obtuse). The angle drawn is a little narrower than a square corner.
misconceptions.2: 10° is a very thin angle, much smaller than the one drawn.
misconceptions.3: 170° is nearly a straight line, much wider than the angle drawn.

questions.prompt: Look at the triangle. Two of its angles are marked. What is the size of the third angle, marked ? on the drawing? Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: The angles in a triangle add up to 180°. 50 + 60 = 110. 180 - 110 = 70°.

misconceptions.common: Using 360° instead of 180° gives 250°, which is impossible inside a triangle. Triangle angles add up to 180°.

questions.prompt: What is the size of each angle in an equilateral triangle?
questions.solution: An equilateral triangle has three equal angles. They add up to 180°, so each is 180 ÷ 3 = 60°.

misconceptions.0: Three right angles would add up to 270°, more than the 180° in a triangle.
misconceptions.1: You shared 360° by 3. The angles in a triangle add up to 180°, not 360°.
misconceptions.2: 180° is the TOTAL of all three angles, not the size of each one.

questions.prompt: True or false: A triangle can have angles of 30°, 60° and 90°.
questions.solution: 30 + 60 + 90 = 180. The angles add up to exactly 180°, so this triangle can exist. It is a right-angled triangle. The statement is true.

misconceptions.common: Not checking the total. The rule is that the three angles of a triangle must add up to exactly 180°.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a right-angled triangle. What is the size of the angle marked ? on the drawing?
questions.solution: The square mark shows a right angle, 90°. The angles add up to 180°. 90 + 34 = 124. 180 - 124 = 56°.

misconceptions.1: You did 180 - 34 but forgot the right angle (the square mark, 90°) is also in the triangle.
misconceptions.2: Slip in 90 - 34. In the ones column 0 - 4 needs an exchange: 90 - 34 = 56.
misconceptions.3: You assumed the two smaller angles are equal. That only happens when the other angle is 45°, not 34°.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows an isosceles triangle. The two sides with a mark are equal. What is the size of each angle marked x?
questions.solution: The 40° angle is between the two equal (marked) sides. The two angles x are equal. 180 - 40 = 140. 140 ÷ 2 = 70°. Check: 40 + 70 + 70 = 180.

misconceptions.0: You found 180 - 40 = 140 but forgot that this is shared between the two equal angles x.
misconceptions.1: You thought all three angles are equal. That is an equilateral triangle, not this one.
misconceptions.3: You treated 40° as one of the two equal angles: 180 - 40 - 40 = 100. Here 40° is the angle BETWEEN the equal sides, so the two angles x are the equal ones.

questions.prompt: True or false: A triangle can have two obtuse angles.
questions.solution: An obtuse angle is more than 90°. Two obtuse angles would add up to more than 180° by themselves, leaving nothing for the third angle. So the statement is false.

misconceptions.common: Not using the 180° rule. Try an example: 100 + 100 = 200, already more than 180°.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows an isosceles triangle. The two sides with a mark are equal. What is the size of the angle marked ? on the drawing?
questions.solution: The two marked sides are equal, so the two angles at the bottom (opposite those sides) are equal: both are 65°. 65 + 65 = 130. 180 - 130 = 50°.

misconceptions.0: You treated 65° as the odd angle and shared the rest: (180 - 65) ÷ 2. But the angle marked ? is between the two equal sides, so the OTHER bottom angle is also 65°.
misconceptions.1: You took away only one 65°. The other bottom angle is also 65°: 180 - 65 - 65 = 50.
misconceptions.3: You thought all three angles are equal, but only the two bottom angles are.

questions.prompt: Look at triangle ABC. Angle C is 72°. Angle A is twice the size of angle B. What is the size of angle B? Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: A + B = 180 - 72 = 108°. Think of B as 1 part and A as 2 parts: 3 parts = 108°. 1 part = 108 ÷ 3 = 36°. So B = 36° (and A = 72°). Check: 36 + 72 + 72 = 180.

misconceptions.common: Halving 108 to get 54° treats A and B as equal. A is twice B, so split 108 into 3 equal parts.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the sets of three angles that could be the angles of a triangle.

misconceptions.1: 60 + 60 + 70 = 190°, which is more than 180°.
misconceptions.3: These add to 180°, but an angle of 0° is not a corner at all, so no triangle can be made.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a right-angled triangle. What is its area? Give your answer in cm².
questions.solution: Use the two sides that meet at the right angle (the square mark): 6 cm and 8 cm. The triangle is half of a 6 cm by 8 cm rectangle. Rectangle: 6 x 8 = 48 cm². Triangle: 48 ÷ 2 = 24 cm².

misconceptions.common: Forgetting to halve gives 48 cm², the area of the whole rectangle. Using the 10 cm side is also wrong: it is opposite the right angle. Use the two sides that meet at the square mark.

questions.prompt: The rectangle shown is cut along the dashed diagonal into two identical right-angled triangles. What is the area of one triangle?
questions.solution: Rectangle area = 10 x 4 = 40 cm². The diagonal cuts it into two equal halves, so each triangle is 40 ÷ 2 = 20 cm².

misconceptions.0: 40 cm² is the area of the whole rectangle. Each triangle is half of it.
misconceptions.2: You added 10 + 4. Area needs multiplying: 10 x 4 = 40, then halve.
misconceptions.3: You halved 10 + 4. Area needs multiplying: 10 x 4 ÷ 2 = 20 cm².

questions.prompt: The right-angled triangle shown has an area of 30 cm². What is the length of the side marked ? on the drawing?
questions.solution: The side marked ? and the 5 cm side meet at the right angle. The triangle is half of a rectangle, so the rectangle's area is 30 x 2 = 60 cm². 60 ÷ 5 = 12 cm. Check: 5 x 12 ÷ 2 = 30.

misconceptions.1: You did 30 ÷ 5 but forgot the triangle is only half a rectangle. The rectangle would be 60 cm², and 60 ÷ 5 = 12 cm.
misconceptions.2: You subtracted 5 from 30. Area comes from multiplying, so work backwards by dividing.
misconceptions.3: You multiplied 30 by 5. To work backwards from an area you divide.

questions.prompt: Look at the right-angled triangle. What is its area?
questions.solution: Use the two sides that meet at the right angle (the square mark): 9 cm and 7 cm. 9 x 7 = 63. 63 ÷ 2 = 31.5 cm². The 11.4 cm side is not needed.

misconceptions.0: You multiplied 9 x 7 but forgot to halve. 63 cm² is the area of the rectangle.
misconceptions.1: You used the longest side (11.4 cm) with 9 cm. Use the two sides that meet at the right angle.
misconceptions.3: You used the longest side (11.4 cm) with 7 cm. Use the two sides that meet at the right angle.

questions.prompt: The shape shown is made of a rectangle and a right-angled triangle, split by the dashed line. What is the total area of the shape? Give your answer in cm².
questions.solution: Rectangle: 8 x 5 = 40 cm². The dashed line is the rectangle's right-hand side, so it is also 5 cm, and it meets the 6 cm side at a right angle. Triangle: 5 x 6 ÷ 2 = 15 cm². Total: 40 + 15 = 55 cm².

misconceptions.common: Forgetting to halve the triangle gives 40 + 30 = 70 cm². Or using the whole bottom (8 + 6 = 14 cm) as a rectangle: 14 x 5 = 70 cm² counts a triangle that is not there.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a square garden. The triangle in the bottom left corner is a flower bed, and the rest of the garden is grass. What is the area of the grass?

diagram.caption: The flower bed is the right-angled triangle in the bottom left corner.

questions.solution: Garden: 10 x 10 = 100 m². Flower bed: a right-angled triangle with sides 6 m and 4 m meeting at the corner of the garden: 6 x 4 ÷ 2 = 12 m². Grass: 100 - 12 = 88 m².

misconceptions.0: You took away 4 x 6 = 24 without halving. The flower bed is a triangle: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 m².
misconceptions.2: You added the flower bed instead of taking it away. The grass is what is left.
misconceptions.3: You took away 4 + 6 = 10. The flower bed's area is 4 x 6 ÷ 2 = 12 m².

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a rectangle of card. A right-angled triangle is cut off the top right corner along the dashed line. What is the area of the card that is left? Give your answer in cm².
questions.solution: Rectangle: 12 x 8 = 96 cm². The triangle cut off has sides 3 cm and 4 cm meeting at the corner: 3 x 4 ÷ 2 = 6 cm². Card left: 96 - 6 = 90 cm².

misconceptions.common: Forgetting to halve the triangle gives 96 - 12 = 84 cm².

questions.prompt: True or false: If two right-angled triangles have the same area, their sides must be the same lengths.
questions.solution: A triangle with shorter sides 4 cm and 6 cm has area 4 x 6 ÷ 2 = 12 cm². A triangle with shorter sides 3 cm and 8 cm has area 3 x 8 ÷ 2 = 12 cm² too, but its sides are different. So the statement is false.

misconceptions.common: Thinking one area can only come from one shape. Many different pairs of sides multiply to the same number.

questions.prompt: The protractor is placed on the angle as shown. What is the size of the angle?
questions.solution: One arm lies along the zero line pointing to the LEFT. Use the scale that starts at 0 on the left (the outer scale). Follow it round to the other arm: it reads 70. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 70° makes sense.

misconceptions.0: It looks like you read the inner scale. That scale starts at 0 on the right, but the arm on the zero line points to the left. Always start from 0 on the arm you lined up. Also, the angle is smaller than a right angle, so it cannot be 110°.
misconceptions.1: You worked out how far the arm is from the 90 mark (90 - 70). The protractor reading already gives the angle: 70°.
misconceptions.2: You took 110 from 360. That is the reflex angle the long way round, not the angle between the arms.

questions.prompt: Look at the protractor placed on the angle shown. What is the size of the angle? Give your answer in degrees.

diagram.alt: A protractor is placed with its centre on the corner of the angle and its baseline along the horizontal. One arm runs along the baseline to the left. The other arm goes up and to the right, crossing the scales halfway between two labelled marks.

questions.solution: The arm on the zero line points to the LEFT, so use the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm is halfway between the marks labelled 150 and 160 on that scale, so it reads 155. Check: the angle is wider than a right angle (obtuse), so an answer between 90° and 180° makes sense. The angle is 155°.

misconceptions.common: Reading 25 from the inner scale. The inner scale starts at 0 on the right, but this angle's arm on the zero line points to the left. The angle is obtuse, so it must be more than 90°. Another slip is reading 165 or 145: the arm is exactly halfway between 150 and 160.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows three angles on a straight line. The small square marks a right angle. What is the size of the angle marked ? on the drawing? Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. The square shows a right angle, 90°. 38 + 90 = 128. 180 - 128 = 52°.

misconceptions.common: Forgetting the right angle: 180 - 38 = 142°. The small square means 90°, and it must be taken away too: 180 - 38 - 90 = 52°.

questions.prompt: Four angles meet at a point, as shown. The small square marks a right angle, and the two angles marked x are equal. What is the size of x?
questions.solution: Angles around a point add up to 360°. The right angle is 90°. 90 + 140 = 230. 360 - 230 = 130. The two equal angles x share 130°: 130 ÷ 2 = 65°. Check: 90 + 140 + 65 + 65 = 360.

misconceptions.0: You found what is left (130°) but forgot to share it between the TWO angles marked x: 130 ÷ 2 = 65°.
misconceptions.2: You left out the right angle. The small square is 90°, so take it away as well: 360 - 90 - 140 = 130, then 130 ÷ 2 = 65°.
misconceptions.3: You used 180° (a straight line) instead of 360°, and missed the right angle. Angles around a point make a full turn, 360°.

questions.prompt: Work out the missing angle, marked ?, in the triangle shown. Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: The angles in a triangle add up to 180°. 47 + 81 = 128. 180 - 128 = 52°. Check: 47 + 81 + 52 = 180.

misconceptions.common: Slips when adding or taking away: 47 + 81 = 128 (7 + 1 = 8, 40 + 80 = 120), then 180 - 128 = 52. Using 360° instead of 180° gives 232°, which is far too big for a corner of a triangle.

questions.prompt: The triangle shown is isosceles: the two sides with a mark are equal. What is the size of the angle marked ? on the drawing?
questions.solution: The two marked sides meet at the top corner. The angles opposite the equal sides are the two bottom angles, so they are equal. The angle marked ? is the same as the other bottom angle: 52°. (The top angle is 180 - 52 - 52 = 76°.)

misconceptions.1: 76° is the TOP angle (180 - 52 - 52). The angle marked ? is a bottom angle, and the two bottom angles are equal because they sit opposite the two equal sides.
misconceptions.2: You treated 52° as the top angle and shared the rest: (180 - 52) ÷ 2 = 64. But 52° is at the bottom, next to the unmarked side, so the other bottom angle is equal to it.
misconceptions.3: You did 180 - 52, as if the two angles were on a straight line. They are two corners of a triangle; here they are equal because the marked sides are equal.

questions.prompt: Triangle PQR is drawn below, with a right angle at Q. Angle P is 28° bigger than angle R. What is the size of angle R? Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: Angle Q is 90°, so P + R = 180 - 90 = 90°. P is 28° more than R. Take the extra 28° away: 90 - 28 = 62. Now P and R would be equal, so share it: 62 ÷ 2 = 31. So R = 31° and P = 31 + 28 = 59°. Check: 90 + 59 + 31 = 180.

misconceptions.common: Answering 59°, which is angle P, the bigger one; R is the smaller angle. Another slip is forgetting the right angle: (180 - 28) ÷ 2 = 76°, which is too big, because P and R must share only 90°.

questions.prompt: Look at the four shapes. Arrows on two sides show that those sides are parallel. Which shape is a trapezium?
questions.solution: A trapezium is a quadrilateral with exactly ONE pair of parallel sides. Shape C has one pair (the top and bottom, marked with arrows) and its slanting sides are not parallel. Shape A has two pairs of parallel sides (a parallelogram), shape B is a kite (no parallel sides) and shape D has no parallel sides.

misconceptions.0: Shape A has TWO pairs of parallel sides (single arrows and double arrows), so it is a parallelogram. A trapezium has exactly one pair.
misconceptions.1: Shape B is a kite: its equal sides (the marks) are next to each other, and it has no parallel sides.
misconceptions.3: Shape D has no parallel sides at all: the top and bottom slope differently. A trapezium needs one pair of parallel sides.

questions.prompt: Look at the five shapes. Matching dashes show equal sides, matching arrows show parallel sides, and small squares show right angles. Select ALL the shapes that are parallelograms.
questions.solution: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides. Shape A has four right angles, so it is a rectangle, and every rectangle is a parallelogram. Shape C has four equal sides, so it is a rhombus, and every rhombus is a parallelogram. Shape E has two pairs of parallel sides (single and double arrows): an ordinary parallelogram. Shape B is a kite (no parallel sides) and shape D is a trapezium (only one pair). Answer: A, C and E.

misconceptions.1: Shape B is a kite: its equal sides are next to each other, not opposite, and none of its sides are parallel.
misconceptions.3: Shape D is a trapezium: it has only ONE pair of parallel sides. A parallelogram needs two pairs.
misconceptions.common: Leaving out shape A or shape C. Rectangles and rhombuses have two pairs of parallel sides, so they are special parallelograms, just as a square is a special rectangle.

questions.prompt: Find the area of the right-angled triangle shown. Give your answer in cm².
questions.solution: Find the right angle first: the square mark is at the top corner. The two sides that meet there are 5 cm and 12 cm. The triangle is half of a 5 cm by 12 cm rectangle: 5 x 12 = 60, and 60 ÷ 2 = 30 cm². The 13 cm side along the bottom is opposite the right angle, so it is not used.

misconceptions.common: Using the 13 cm side because it is at the bottom: 13 x 5 ÷ 2 = 32.5 or 13 x 12 ÷ 2 = 78. The two sides you multiply must meet at the right angle (the square mark), here 5 cm and 12 cm. Forgetting to halve gives 60 cm².

questions.prompt: The shape shown is made of a rectangle and a right-angled triangle, split by the dashed line. Work out the area of the whole shape. Give your answer in cm².
questions.solution: Rectangle (left of the dashed line): 7 cm wide and 9 cm tall, so 7 x 9 = 63 cm². Triangle (right of the dashed line): its height is the dashed line, 9 cm, and its bottom side is 12 - 7 = 5 cm. Area = 5 x 9 ÷ 2 = 22.5 cm². Total: 63 + 22.5 = 85.5 cm².

misconceptions.common: Using 12 cm as the triangle's bottom side. The 12 cm is the WHOLE bottom; the rectangle takes 7 cm of it, so the triangle's part is 12 - 7 = 5 cm. Forgetting to halve the triangle gives 63 + 45 = 108 cm².

questions.prompt: The right-angled triangle is drawn on squared paper. Each square is 1 cm by 1 cm. What is the area of the triangle?
questions.solution: Count the squares along the two sides that meet at the right angle: 6 along the bottom and 4 up the side. The triangle is half of a 6 by 4 rectangle. 6 x 4 = 24. 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cm².

misconceptions.0: 24 cm² is the whole 6 by 4 rectangle. The triangle is only half of it: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cm².
misconceptions.1: You added 6 + 4. Area needs multiplying: 6 x 4 = 24, then halve to get 12 cm².
misconceptions.2: 20 is the perimeter of the 6 by 4 rectangle (6 + 4 + 6 + 4). Area is the space inside: 6 x 4 ÷ 2 = 12 cm².

questions.prompt: Look at the circle. Its diameter is 18 cm, as marked. What is the length of the radius marked ? on the drawing? Give your answer in cm.
questions.solution: The radius goes from the centre to the edge: half of the diameter. Radius = 18 ÷ 2 = 9 cm.

misconceptions.common: Doubling instead of halving gives 36 cm. The radius is the SHORTER line, from the centre to the edge, so it is half the diameter: 18 ÷ 2 = 9 cm.

questions.prompt: O is the centre of the circle shown. Wei Ming says the straight line AB is a diameter because it joins two points on the edge of the circle. True or false: Wei Ming is right.

diagram.alt: A circle with centre O. Points A and B are on the circle, joined by a straight line.

questions.solution: A diameter must go from edge to edge THROUGH the centre. In the drawing, AB passes above the centre O, not through it. So AB is not a diameter (it is a chord, and it is shorter than a diameter). The statement is false.

misconceptions.common: Thinking any line from edge to edge is a diameter. Check whether it goes through the centre O: AB misses O, so it is a chord, not a diameter.

questions.prompt: Look at the four drawings. In each one, look at the angle that is marked. Which marked angle is a reflex angle?

optionDiagrams.alt: Two arms, one pointing right and one pointing up and to the left. The angle between them is marked on the inside.
Two arms, one pointing right and one pointing up and to the left. The angle is marked on the outside, going round from the arm pointing up and to the left, past the bottom, to the arm pointing right.
Two arms, one pointing right and one pointing straight up, with a small square marked between them.
Two arms, one pointing right and one pointing left and a little up. The angle between them is marked on the inside.

questions.solution: A reflex angle is more than 180° (more than a straight line) and less than 360°. In B the arc goes the long way round, from one arm, under the corner, to the other arm: that is 360 - 110 = 250°, a reflex angle. A (120°) and D (170°) are obtuse, and C is a right angle (the square mark).

misconceptions.0: Angle A is wider than a right angle but less than a straight line, so it is obtuse. A reflex angle goes past a straight line.
misconceptions.2: The small square means a right angle, exactly 90°. A reflex angle is more than 180°.
misconceptions.3: Angle D is nearly a straight line, but it is still less than 180°, so it is obtuse. Look for the arc that goes the long way round.
